entities.summary:
Flavius Timasius (died 396 CE) was a high-ranking Roman general of Gothic or Thracian origin, a pivotal military figure in the Eastern Roman Empire during the late 4th century. His career, spanning the reigns of Emperors Valens and Theodosius I, saw him rise through the ranks to magister equitum and magister peditum, commanding significant portions of the Roman army. His familial connection to Empress Aelia Flaccilla, wife of Theodosius I, further cemented his influence, placing him at the heart of imperial politics and military strategy during a tumultuous period marked by Gothic incursions and internal power struggles that shaped the empire's eventual division.

Timasius distinguished himself early in his career, notably participating in the catastrophic Battle of Adrianople in 378 CE, though he survived and helped reorganize the shattered legions. Under Theodosius I, he became one of the emperor's most trusted generals, playing a crucial role in the campaign against the usurper Magnus Maximus in the West. He led the Eastern Roman forces at the decisive Battle of the Save (Sava) in 388 CE, contributing significantly to Theodosius's victory and the brief reunification of the empire. After Theodosius's death in 395 CE, Timasius served the young Emperor Arcadius, attempting to maintain stability in the East amidst the growing influence of figures like the eunuch Eutropius.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Timasius was a crucial military commander whose victories helped consolidate Theodosius I's reign and briefly reunify the Roman Empire. His career and subsequent downfall exemplify the shifting power dynamics between military leaders and court eunuchs in the late 4th-century Eastern Roman Empire.
